title: Given an inventory or stock scenario, how do you decide between optimistic and pessimistic locking based on conflict frequency and the trade-offs involved?
shortTitle: Optimistic vs pessimistic by conflict frequency?

s1_definition.profdef: The choice between optimistic and pessimistic locking is a function of contention. When many concurrent writers target the same row (high conflict probability), pessimistic locking avoids repeated failed retries. When writers rarely collide (low conflict probability), optimistic locking maximizes throughput by never holding locks and only paying a cost in the rare conflict case. The crossover point is where the cost of retries under optimism exceeds the cost of serialized waiting under pessimism.
s1_definition.analogy: Picture National Bank of India's brokerage selling units of a hot IPO. If only one popular stock has 10 units left and 5,000 investors click "buy" in the same second, that single row is red hot — optimistic locking would cause thousands of retries and a storm of failures. Pessimistic locking lines everyone up neatly. But for Rajesh buying a sleepy, rarely traded bond, almost no one else touches that row, so optimistic locking is perfect and far faster.
s1_definition.oneliner: Hot row with many writers → pessimistic; cold row with rare clashes → optimistic.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The choice between optimistic and pessimistic locking is a function of contention. When many concurrent writers target the same row (high conflict probability), pessimistic locking avoids repeated failed retries. When writers rarely collide (low conflict probability), optimistic locking maximizes throughput by never holding locks and only paying a cost in the rare conflict case. The crossover point is where the cost of retries under optimism exceeds the cost of serialized waiting under pessimism.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Picture National Bank of India's brokerage selling units of a hot IPO. If only one popular stock has 10 units left and 5,000 investors click "buy" in the same second, that single row is red hot — optimistic locking would cause thousands of retries and a storm of failures. Pessimistic locking lines everyone up neatly. But for Rajesh buying a sleepy, rarely traded bond, almost no one else touches that row, so optimistic locking is perfect and far faster.

**One line to remember:** Hot row with many writers → pessimistic; cold row with rare clashes → optimistic.

sections.s2_technical:
Conflict probability is the deciding factor. For a stock with quantity decrementing, if the arrival rate of concurrent buy requests on the same symbol is high, optimistic locking produces a cascade: many transactions read quantity=10, all try to decrement, one succeeds, the rest hit version conflicts and retry — and on retry they conflict again. This is a livelock risk and burns CPU and database round-trips.

Pessimistic locking on the same hot symbol serializes access: `SELECT quantity FROM stock WHERE symbol=? FOR UPDATE`. Each request waits its turn, decrements, commits. Throughput per row is bounded by lock-hold time but there is no wasted work.

For a cold symbol rarely bought concurrently, optimistic locking wins: no lock overhead, and the rare conflict costs one cheap retry. Holding a pessimistic lock here would needlessly reduce concurrency and risk lock-wait timeouts on the connection pool.

A hybrid pattern many systems use is atomic conditional update: `UPDATE stock SET quantity = quantity - :q WHERE symbol = :s AND quantity >= :q`. This pushes the check-and-decrement into one atomic SQL statement, eliminating the read-modify-write race entirely without an explicit application-held lock. If zero rows update, the stock was insufficient.

Senior nuances: you can measure conflict rate in production (retry counter metric) and adapt. For extreme hot keys you may shard the quantity into N sub-rows to spread contention, or move to a queue that serializes orders per symbol. The right answer in interviews is: measure contention, prefer optimistic by default, escalate to pessimistic or atomic SQL for proven hot rows.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India's brokerage lists a hot IPO stock with only 10 units. Thousands of clients, including Rajesh and Priya, try to buy in the same second. If we read-modify-write with optimistic locking, almost everyone conflicts and retries, flooding the database. This is the high-contention case that argues for pessimistic locking or atomic SQL.

Problem 2 — The same brokerage lists a thinly traded government bond. Rajesh buys 5 units; nobody else is buying at that moment. Here optimistic locking is ideal — no lock overhead, essentially never a conflict.

Problem 3 — We want a bulletproof decrement that cannot oversell even under extreme load. This is the atomic conditional UPDATE pattern.

We will build a StockService offering optimistic buy, pessimistic buy, and an atomic-decrement buy, so we can pick per symbol.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: 3 concurrent buys of 4 units each on HOTIPO (only 10 units); one buy of 5 on GOVTBOND.

Step 1 — Under optimistic buying on HOTIPO, all three read quantity 10, version 0. The first commits (quantity 6, version 1). The other two conflict, retry, read 6, one commits (quantity 2), the last reads 2 and retries again — heavy churn.

Step 2 — Under pessimistic buying, buyer A locks HOTIPO via FOR UPDATE, reduces to 6, commits. Buyer B waited, now locks, reduces to 2, commits. Buyer C waits, locks, tries to reduce by 4 but only 2 left — throws out-of-stock. Clean, no wasted retries.

Step 3 — Under atomic buying, each request runs `UPDATE ... SET quantity=quantity-4 WHERE quantity>=4`. First updates 1 row (10 to 6), second updates 1 row (6 to 2), third updates 0 rows (2 < 4) and returns false. No lost updates, no retries.

Step 4 — GOVTBOND optimistic buy reads version 0, reduces by 5, commits version 1 — zero conflicts because no one else is trading it.

```
WARNING  Conflict on HOTIPO retry 1
INFO  Pessimistic buy HOTIPO x4
WARNING  Oversell blocked: HOTIPO
INFO  GOVTBOND optimistic buy x5 committed (no conflict)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
This is fundamentally a contention question, so my answer always starts with "it depends on how often two writers hit the same row." When many concurrent buyers target one hot row, optimistic locking backfires: everyone reads the same version, one succeeds, the rest fail and retry, and on retry they conflict again, which wastes CPU and database round-trips and can even livelock. For a hot row I therefore prefer pessimistic locking with select-for-update, which serializes buyers cleanly so each one waits its turn and no work is wasted.

When writers rarely collide, optimistic locking is the clear winner. It holds no locks, scales well, and the rare conflict costs just one cheap retry. Holding a pessimistic lock on a cold row would only reduce concurrency and risk lock-wait timeouts on the connection pool for no benefit.

In our National Bank of India brokerage, a hot IPO with only ten units and thousands of simultaneous buyers is the high-contention case, so I use pessimistic locking or, even better, an atomic conditional update that decrements quantity in a single statement with a where-quantity-greater-or-equal guard. That atomic approach eliminates the read-modify-write race entirely and simply reports zero rows updated when stock is insufficient, so we can never oversell. For a thinly traded government bond that almost no one buys concurrently, I use optimistic locking because conflicts essentially never happen.

The principled position I give in interviews is: default to optimistic because it scales, measure the per-symbol conflict rate in production with a retry counter, and escalate specific proven hot rows to pessimistic locking or atomic SQL. For truly extreme hot keys I go further and either shard the quantity across several sub-rows to spread contention or route orders for that symbol through a queue that serializes them. The goal is correctness first, then the highest throughput the contention profile allows.

---

keyPoints: Low conflict (read-heavy): optimistic — no locks, fast
High conflict (write-heavy): pessimistic — prevents conflicts upfront
Optimistic failure: OptimisticLockException — retry the operation
Pessimistic: potential deadlocks if lock ordering is wrong
